summary: Suggests a way to use DNS to find the network that contains a given IP address, its netmask, and the addresses of first-hop routers. It supports variable-length subnet masks, subnets on non-octet boundaries, and multiple routers per subnet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If you know a house number, you might want to know the street, its size and the exits. This memo suggests asking the phone-book-like DNS system for those details.

questions: dns lookup of network and netmask
how do you find a network from an ip address using dns
how do you publish network information in dns
subtitle: Using DNS to find the network containing an IP address and its first-hop routers.

tldr.problem: Network services sometimes need to find the network that contains a host IP address, along with the network's size and first-hop routers. This information is not easily available from the IP address alone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC suggests using DNS PTR records with specially-formatted domain names (based on CIDR notation) to store and query this network information. Lookups start with a /24 assumption and adjust based on returned results.
tldr.outcome: This method supports variable-length subnet masks and non-octet-boundary delegation, fixing limitations in earlier DNS-based approaches like RFC 1101.

today: RFC 4183 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes a method that organizations can use to publish network and router information via DNS, though adoption has been limited.

sections.title: Why Find Networks via DNS
sections.content: Third-party network servers sometimes need to provide services specific to a host. To do this, they need to know which network the host belongs to, what the network's netmask is, and which routers serve that network. DNS provides a global, distributed way to store such information. This RFC extends earlier DNS-based approaches (RFC 1101) to support modern networking practices like variable-length subnet masks that are now common on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Some servers need to know about a host's neighborhood: which network it is on, how big that network is, and which routers lead out of it. DNS is a good place to look this up.

sections.title: Encoding Networks in DNS Domain Names
sections.content:
Networks are encoded as special domain names under the in-addr.arpa. hierarchy. Each network is represented using a format like 0-26.2.100.10.in-addr.arpa., where the first label combines an octet value with a mask length (for example, 0-26 means the octet value 0 with a 26-bit mask, representing a /26 network). This format, based on RFC 2317's classless delegation approach, allows networks at any bit boundary to be represented, not just at octet boundaries.

The hyphen delimiter is used instead of the slash (/) to avoid compatibility problems with DNS servers that treat slash as a hostname separator.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks get special names in DNS that look like a reversed IP address with a number-and-dash at the start. The dash separates the network's starting octet from how many bits define it.

sections.title: Looking Up a Network for an IP Address
sections.content:
The lookup procedure works step-by-step. First, a client assumes the IP address belongs to a /24 network and constructs a DNS domain name for it. It then performs a PTR lookup. If the result is another network domain name (not a hostname), the client reduces it to canonical form, checks if the original IP falls within that subnet, and repeats the lookup for the narrower network. This continues until a PTR lookup returns hostnames instead of network domain names; these are treated as the first-hop routers for that network.

If a PTR lookup fails, the procedure adjusts the netmask: it tries /16, /8, and progressively narrower masks, or increases the mask width by 1 bit, depending on which netmasks have already succeeded, until it either finds the network or exhausts all possibilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Start by guessing the IP is on a medium-sized network. Ask DNS about it. If DNS says it is actually on a smaller network that contains the IP, ask about that smaller one. Keep asking about smaller networks until DNS gives you the names of the routers instead of another network.

sections.title: Non-Octet-Boundary Delegation
sections.content: The method supports a powerful feature: networks can be delegated at non-octet boundaries. For example, an organization controlling 10.1.0.0/16 might delegate only 10.1.0.0/18 to another entity. The delegating organization can set up an NS record pointing to the other entity's DNS server for 0-18.1.10.in-addr.arpa.. The other entity can then further subnet this into 10.1.0.0/25 and define it as 0-25.0.0-18.1.10.in-addr.arpa. in their own DNS. The client can reduce such non-canonical names by dropping intermediate masked-octet labels to find the canonical form.
sections.plainLanguage: One organization can hand off partial control of its network to another, even at odd boundaries. The delegated parts can use longer, nested names that include hints about the delegation chain.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content: Exposing network structure and router addresses in public DNS can reveal information about internal network design to potential attackers. Organizations should carefully control which DNS records are visible to the public Internet and which are kept private. Alternatively, organizations that do not wish to participate in a public network DNS can use an alternate domain suffix (such as in-addr.example.com. instead of in-addr.arpa.) for internal use while maintaining the standard approach where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing network details in DNS might help attackers understand your network layout. Keep this information private unless you decide the benefits of sharing it are worth the risk.
